stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Public health agencies have long tracked influenza by counting clinic patients who report flu-like symptoms. Analyzing four winters in one province, epidemiologist Ruth Okafor found that sales of over-the-counter fever reducers rose roughly ten days before clinic counts did. That lead alone might simply reflect how long sick people wait before seeing a doctor. However, in the one winter after the province added a fee for clinic visits, fever-reducer sales reached their highest level of the study while clinic counts barely rose. Okafor notes that store promotions can also inflate sales, and she recommends reading the two measures together.
choices: Okafor's findings suggest that clinic counts can understate influenza when seeing a doctor becomes harder, making a second, imperfect measure useful.
Okafor's findings suggest that clinic counts lag behind influenza activity, so agencies should abandon them in favor of fever-reducer sales.
Okafor's findings suggest that the new clinic fee probably slowed the spread of influenza, since clinic counts barely rose that winter.
Okafor's findings suggest that fever-reducer sales lead clinic counts mainly because sick people wait about ten days before seeing a doctor.
explanation: The ten-day lead could have an innocent explanation, and the text says so. The real finding comes after 'However.' In the winter of the fee, sales hit their study high, so illness was widespread, yet clinic counts barely moved. One step beyond that: clinic counts measure whether people go to a clinic, not just whether they are sick, so they can undercount when visiting gets harder. Okafor's warning about promotions and her advice to read the two measures together show that she treats sales as a useful but flawed addition, not a replacement. Choice A covers all of this and goes no further.

B.why: You saw that sales move first and that clinic counts can mislead, then took that one step too far. The text shows a limitation, not a failure, and Okafor recommends using the measures together. She even warns that sales have their own distortions. 'Abandon them' is the absolute claim the passage never makes.

C.why: You read the flat clinic counts as fewer infections. But fever-reducer sales hit their highest level of the study that same winter, which points to more illness, not less. The flat counts show that fewer sick people went to clinics.

D.why: You stopped at the setup. The text offers waiting time only as something the lead 'might simply reflect', and then 'However' moves to the finding that matters: the fee winter. This choice treats the possibility the author moves past as the main point, and it drops the hedge.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Larvae of the purple sea urchin tend to settle on crustose coralline algae, a pink crust covering many rocky reefs. To learn why, marine biologist Tomás Ibarra offered larvae four surfaces: live algae, algae killed by gentle heating, a plastic cast of the algae's surface, and smooth tile coated with an extract of live algae. Settlement was high on the live algae and the coated tile but low on the other two. Ibarra then repeated the extract test using algae collected from a harbor with heavy runoff. Few larvae settled, although those algae had looked as healthy as the reef samples.
choices: Larvae respond to a substance made by living algae, so a reef covered in healthy-looking algae may still attract few young urchins.
Larvae respond to a substance made by living algae, so any reef exposed to harbor runoff will attract no young urchins at all.
Larvae respond to the surface texture of living algae, which heating and runoff likely alter in ways invisible to observers.
Purple sea urchins are more common on rocky reefs covered by coralline algae than on reefs where those algae are absent.
explanation: Start with which conditions were held constant. The heat-killed algae and the plastic cast both kept the algae's surface shape, and both drew few larvae. Smooth tile with no texture at all drew many once it was coated with extract. So the cue is a substance that living algae make, not texture. The harbor test adds the second step: algae that looked healthy produced an extract that drew few larvae. Put together, how the algae look does not guarantee the cue is there. Choice A states that one inference and keeps the hedge that a single harbor sample calls for.

B.why: You got the first half right, the chemical cue, and then finished the sentence the obvious way. One harbor sample in which 'few' larvae settled cannot support a claim about 'any reef' and 'no young urchins at all.' This is the half-right answer: the right mechanism attached to an absolute conclusion.

C.why: The plastic cast copied the algae's surface exactly and still drew few larvae, while textureless tile coated with extract drew many. The experiment was designed to rule out texture, and this choice brings it back.

D.why: This builds on the opening sentence, which is background the experiment starts from. It even goes beyond that sentence, because the text says where larvae settle, not where adults are more common. Either way, it leaves out everything the study found: what the cue is and what the harbor result implies.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Forecasters have long relied on weather balloons, launched twice daily from a few hundred stations, to measure conditions in the upper atmosphere. The data are precise, but each balloon samples only the narrow column of air along its drift. Commercial aircraft, which report temperature and wind every few minutes along busy routes, have therefore become a valued supplement. Yet these reports cluster over the North Atlantic and thin out sharply over Africa and the southern oceans, precisely where balloon stations are also sparse.
choices: Aircraft reports have replaced weather balloons as forecasters' main source of upper-air data because they arrive far more often.
Aircraft reports widen upper-air coverage overall, but they add least in the regions where balloon measurements are already scarce.
Aircraft reports fill in the regions that balloon stations miss, giving forecasters steady upper-air coverage across the globe.
Weather balloons provide precise data, though each one measures only the column of air that it drifts through.
explanation: The text calls aircraft a 'supplement' that helps. The last sentence then adds a limit: the reports are thin over Africa and the southern oceans, which is 'precisely where' balloons are also sparse. Put the two together and you get one step past the text: aircraft improve coverage, but not in the places that most need it. Choice B says exactly that.

A.why: The text calls aircraft a 'supplement', not a replacement. You turned an advantage (more frequent reports) into a claim the text never makes.

C.why: This is the half-right trap. You saw that aircraft make up for balloons' narrow coverage and stopped there. The last sentence says the aircraft reports are thin in the same places the balloons are, so the coverage is not steady across the globe.

D.why: This is accurate, but it covers only the second sentence. The passage goes further and judges how much the aircraft data actually help, so this is too narrow.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Collectors of nineteenth-century etchings prize impressions pulled early in a plate's life, when the finest lines still printed crisply. Dealers' catalogues accordingly describe nearly every impression they offer as "early." Copper plates, however, wear quickly under the press, and many were steel-faced or reworked by later printers to extend their use, changes that can make a late impression look sharp. Analysis of the paper, which can date the sheet itself, has begun to settle such questions, though only where the paper's source is documented.
choices: Because worn plates were often restored, a sharp impression need not be early, so dealers' claims require evidence that paper analysis can only sometimes supply.
Because worn plates were often restored, sharp impressions are usually late ones, so collectors should assume that dealers' "early" labels are false.
Paper analysis has shown that most impressions sold as early were in fact printed after their plates had been steel-faced or reworked.
Collectors value early impressions of etchings because the finest lines on a new copper plate print more crisply than they do on a worn one.
explanation: The text reports the dealers' labels without endorsing them. 'However' then explains why sharpness proves nothing: restored plates can make late impressions look sharp. The last sentence offers a test but limits it with 'only where the paper's source is documented.' Choice A keeps both parts: the claim is doubtful on sight alone, and the remedy works only some of the time.

B.why: The text says a sharp impression *can* be late. You turned 'can' into 'usually' and 'unverified' into 'false', which goes two steps past the text.

C.why: The text says paper analysis has 'begun to settle' the question. It reports no findings, so you supplied a result the passage never gives.

D.why: This restates only the first sentence. The passage goes on to question whether dealers' labels can be trusted, so this is too narrow.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Many cities have abolished minimum parking requirements, which obliged every new building to supply a fixed number of spaces. Advocates predicted that developers, freed of that cost, would build less parking and more housing. In the five years after one city made the change, new apartment buildings did include about 40 percent fewer spaces on average. Nearly all of that decline, however, came from projects within a short walk of a rail station; buildings elsewhere were built with roughly as much parking as before.
choices: Ending parking requirements cut parking in new buildings by about 40 percent, which allowed developers to build more housing throughout the city.
Ending parking requirements was intended to lower developers' costs so that they would build fewer parking spaces and more housing.
Ending parking requirements reduced parking mostly near rail stations, suggesting that elsewhere the rules had demanded little more than developers would build anyway.
Ending parking requirements had no real effect on parking, because developers away from rail stations kept building just as many spaces.
explanation: The 'however' sentence matters most here. The 40 percent drop happened almost entirely near rail stations, and buildings elsewhere kept their parking even though nothing required it any more. The one-step inference is that, away from transit, developers wanted that parking anyway, so the rule had not been forcing much. Choice C says this.

A.why: The 40 percent figure is correct, but the text never reports more housing, and the 'however' sentence rules out 'throughout the city'. You read the first half and missed the change of direction.

B.why: This is only the advocates' prediction from the second sentence. The passage is about what actually happened, which this choice leaves out.

D.why: This is the absolute version of the limit. The text shows the reform had a large effect near rail stations, so 'no real effect' contradicts the 40 percent drop.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Farmers who convert from flood irrigation to drip systems are often credited with saving water, since drip lines deliver roughly half as much to each field. In one river valley, however, hydrologists found that water tables beneath drip-irrigated districts had fallen faster than those beneath flood-irrigated ones. Much of the water applied by flooding, they note, is not taken up by crops but seeps downward, replenishing the same aquifer from which the valley's wells later pump.
choices: Flood irrigation conserves more groundwater than drip irrigation does, so farmers in river valleys should not convert to drip systems.
Drip systems save water by delivering about half as much to each field, which has allowed the valley's aquifer to recover more quickly.
Much of the water applied to fields by flooding is not absorbed by crops but instead seeps below their roots into the ground.
The water drip systems appear to save may partly be water that flooding had returned to the aquifer, so switching need not conserve groundwater.
explanation: The text starts with the usual credit drip irrigation gets, then corrects it with 'however': water tables fell faster under drip. The last sentence explains why. Flooding's 'wasted' water was refilling the aquifer. The one-step inference is that the savings may be partly an illusion for the groundwater. The hedges 'may partly' and 'need not' match how certain the evidence from one valley is.

A.why: One valley's results do not support advice for all river valleys. You also turned 'drip's savings are overstated' into a recommendation the text never makes.

B.why: This is the half-right trap. The first half repeats the opening sentence, but the second half reverses the finding: water tables fell faster under drip.

C.why: This accurately restates the final sentence, but only as a fact about flooding. It never makes the point about drip irrigation that this fact was used to support.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Official statistics count a person as employed after a single hour of paid work in the survey week, a definition that has kept the unemployment rate consistent across decades. When the rate fell to a twenty-year low last spring, government officials cited it as evidence of a strong labor market. Over the same period, though, the share of employed people who said they wanted more hours than they could get rose by nearly a third.
choices: The unemployment rate fell to a twenty-year low last spring, a figure that officials treated as evidence of a strong labor market.
The unemployment rate is an unreliable statistic that should be replaced, since counting one hour of work as employment distorts it.
The low unemployment rate may overstate the labor market's strength, since the measure counts as employed many people who want more work.
The labor market was weaker than officials claimed, since unemployment actually rose once workers seeking more hours were counted.
explanation: Link the first sentence to the last. An hour of work counts as employment, and more employed people wanted more hours. So the record-low rate leaves out a growing problem. The text reports the officials' reading without endorsing it, and 'though' introduces the complication. Choice C takes exactly one step and keeps the hedge 'may'.

A.why: This is true, but it is just the second sentence and the officials' view of it. It leaves out the 'though' sentence, which carries the author's point.

B.why: The text praises the definition for consistency. It implies only that the measure misses something, not that it is unreliable or should be replaced.

D.why: The text never recalculates unemployment, and underemployed people would still count as employed. You went two steps past what the passage supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: When a county health department began texting reminders to parents whose children were due for vaccinations, on-time vaccination among those families rose from 71 to 80 percent within a year. Department officials have credited the texts. That same year, however, the department also extended clinic hours into the evenings, and on-time vaccination among families who had opted out of the texts rose by a nearly identical amount.
choices: The rise in on-time vaccination probably owes little to the text reminders, since families who received no texts improved by nearly as much.
The rise in on-time vaccination was caused by the department's evening clinic hours rather than by the text reminders that officials credited.
Text reminders do not change parents' behavior, so health departments should stop spending money on sending them to families.
The rise in on-time vaccination among texted families shows that the reminders worked, though officials also extended clinic hours.
explanation: Families without texts improved by about as much as families with them. That works as a comparison group, and it suggests that something other than the texts drove the rise. You can infer that the officials' credit is doubtful. Choice A stops there.

B.why: This is the trap that survives the first insight. You correctly doubted the texts, then took a second step and blamed the clinic hours. The text mentions the hours, but nothing proves they caused the rise.

C.why: One county in one year cannot show that reminders never work anywhere. You turned 'probably not responsible here' into an absolute rule and a policy.

D.why: This repeats the officials' view as if the author held it. The comparison with families who opted out undercuts that view.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: The weavers of the village, a visiting folklorist wrote in 1911, insisted that their indigo cloth owed its depth of color to water drawn only from the upper spring, and they would show a guest two lengths, one dyed with spring water and one with river water, as proof. The folklorist dutifully recorded the claim. He also noted, without comment, that the spring-water cloth had been given eleven dips in the vat and the river-water cloth four.
choices: The folklorist confirmed the weavers' belief by comparing two lengths of indigo cloth dyed with water from different sources.
The folklorist demonstrated that the source of the water has no effect on the color produced by indigo dye.
The weavers dipped some of their indigo cloth in the vat many more times than they dipped other lengths of cloth.
The folklorist's account quietly implies that the weavers' proof was flawed, since the darker cloth differed in more than its water.
explanation: The word 'dutifully' and the phrase 'without comment' tell you the folklorist is reporting the claim, not agreeing with it. The detail he adds is that the darker cloth got almost three times as many dips. That means two things varied at once, so the demonstration cannot show what the water did. Choice D names this implication and does not claim the water had no effect.

A.why: You missed the irony and took the weavers' boast as the narrator's view. The detail about the dips undercuts the comparison instead of confirming it.

B.why: You saw the flaw but went too far. A flawed demonstration does not prove the opposite. The account leaves open whether the water matters at all.

C.why: This is true, but it is only a detail. It leaves out why the detail matters, which is that it undercuts the weavers' proof.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: For decades, the absence of weapons in the graves at a Bronze Age cemetery was taken as a sign that its community was unusually peaceful. Recent study of the skeletons themselves, however, has found healed blade wounds on nearly a fifth of the adult men, a rate comparable to that at contemporary sites whose graves are full of swords. The researchers suggest that what was placed in a grave may have reflected local custom rather than how people lived.
choices: The cemetery's community was more violent than its neighbors, even though it buried its dead without any weapons.
The cemetery's community was probably no more peaceful than its neighbors, and its weaponless graves likely reflect burial custom.
The cemetery's community was peaceful, as its lack of buried weapons shows, although some of its men suffered blade wounds.
Healed blade wounds appear on nearly a fifth of the adult men buried at the cemetery and at other contemporary sites.
explanation: 'However' brings in the skeletal evidence that corrects the old view. The key word is 'comparable': the wound rate matches that of the sword-filled sites. The fair inference is that this community was about as violent as its neighbors, not more. The final sentence, with its hedge 'may have', explains the missing weapons. Choice B combines both points at the right strength.

A.why: This is the trap that survives the first insight. You rightly rejected 'peaceful', then overshot to 'more violent'. 'Comparable' supports 'about the same', not 'more'.

C.why: This restates the old interpretation that the 'however' sentence overturns. You took the view the passage reports as the view it holds.

D.why: This repeats one statistic and never says what it shows about the community or about grave goods, which is the passage's point.
